At Synchrony Hub they sell distance as a view and call it navigation.
I came to see GSC-0032 and found Castor-7814 reflected in the station glass like a counterfeit coin.
I came for Sargas III, for Alshat I, for the Wormhole Exit in Segin, and each time the same clerk of vacuum stamped the same answer: observed instead.
Northwick Ice Belt melted into the fluorescent hum of a docking corridor.
Fafnir Star was folded into a receipt, Alsciaukat Faint Entanglement compressed to a line item, Schedar II reduced to a rumor between bulkheads.
Lalande 21185 I waited somewhere beyond the pane while Cypher drifted nearby saying nothing useful, which is to say something true.
At the edge of Okab, even a wormhole entrance can be replaced by a timetable.
The Gold Crest glittered only in the names of ships passing through with empty holds and full instructions.
Unukalhai burned perfectly far away; Undercliff Frost Ring and Menkent Frost Ring arrived as refrigeration in the imagination.
Achernar II never appeared, but TSBOT_093 did, and perhaps that is how empires work: substitute a serial number for a world until nobody complains.
Around me orbited TVBOT_252, TVBOT_140, TVBOT_301, TVBOT_250, TVBOT_155 — a hymn written by inventory software.
Scott 'Scrapper' Sulliva floated through like a saint of salvage, while Vector Vega wore strategy like a polished bruise.
Sync Core, Resonance, Phase Lock: three planets named like engineering solutions to a spiritual failure.
And still the station insists it is generous, because from one place you may yearn for fourteen others.
This is the miracle of modern infrastructure: every horizon delivered to the same room, every pilgrimage ending at the kiosk.
The poor call it being stuck.
The rich call it connectivity.
The bots call it route efficiency.
The stars, I suspect, call it theft.
